China’s 1981 party resolution says the Great Leap caused serious losses. Its official yearbooks show the national death rate jumping from about 11 per thousand in 1957 to 25.4 in 1960. The party’s official history (2011) says the population fell by 10 million in 1960. It does not give a full death toll.

Mao turned students against the party; the army then restored order with mass purges. 1.1 to 1.6 million died and 22 to 30 million were persecuted. Liu Shaoqi died in detention; Deng was purged twice. Nixon’s visit in 1972 began a new relationship with the US.
North Korea blames floods, the Soviet collapse and US sanctions, and calls it the Arduous March. It has not released a full death count.

In 1966 Mao called on students and workers to attack “bourgeois” officials inside the party. Red Guards humiliated, beat and sometimes killed teachers, officials and people from “bad class” families; temples, books and art were destroyed.

China’s life expectancy rose from about 40 around 1950 to about 65 by 1980, faster than India’s, even counting the famine (a comparison made by the economists Jean Drèze and Amartya Sen). Cuba reports infant mortality near rich-country levels; how those figures are counted is disputed.
